# Introduction

Cancer classification, using RNA sequencing, is now part of modern precision 
oncology. For some cancers, RNA classification provides deep insights into 
tumor aggressiveness and growth rates. For example, breast cancer subtypes 
(like Luminal-A, Luminal-B, HER2-enriched, or Basal-like) help forecast 
patient outcomes [@Cascianelli2020]. The Luminal-A is the most 
common molecular subtype of breast cancer, making up to 60% of all breast 
cancer cases. It also is associated with good prognosis. While 
Luminal-B tumors have a more aggressive phenotype and a worse 
prognosis [@Yersal2014]. Once gene signatures for RNA subtyping become 
widely accepted by major oncology organizations, they start to classify cancer 
subtypes, predict patient survival, and guide treatment.

From a research aspect, the classification of new samples using their 
transcriptional profiles can be done using different tools. For some cancers, 
machine learning models and dedicated software are available such as 
the Bioconductor Genefu package for breast cancer molecular 
subtyping [@Gendoo2016], and the CMScaller package for subtyping of 
colorectal cancer [@Eide2017].

In the absence of dedicated software, unsupervised clustering with a 
heatmap visualization to classify transcriptomic samples with a 
gene signature is often employed. This method is relatively simple and 
offers an instant visual support. However, this method has a few drawbacks:

* _Lack of statistical metrics_: It doesn't 
provide a statistical probability score for a sample's class assignment; it 
mainly acts as a visual summary. 
* _Metric sensitivity_: Changing the clustering metric (ex: from "Euclidean" to 
"Pearson" distance) can alter the resulting clusters. 
* _Outlier distortion_: Extreme outliers can squash the color scale, and 
artificially create skewed subsets.

The __`r Rpackage("splitTypeR")`__ package resolves these issues by providing 
an automated statistical framework to classify heterogeneous biological 
samples based on gene signature lists, effectively isolating the 
signature-positive samples. 

This classification method is designed for bulk transcriptomic datasets.

<br />

# Installation

As with any R package, the `r Rpackage("splitTypeR")` package should first be 
loaded with the following command:

```{r loadingPackage, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(splitTypeR)
```

<br />

# Method
  
The following figure represents the statistical method employed to turn a noisy, 
single-number enrichment score into a confident binary classification of 
each sample. In summary, the method builds a confidence interval around the 
enrichment score, models the cohort as a mixture of two biological states, and 
then statistically tests each sample against that mixture.


```{r piplineSchema, echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width="100%", fig.cap="General workflow."}
knitr::include_graphics("enrichment_pipeline_300dpi_crop2.jpg")
```
<br />

The statistical method is split into 5 steps. Each of those steps are 
performed for one specific signature at the time. A signature is typically a 
predefined set of features (transcriptomic expression in this situation) that 
is associated with some biological state, pathway, or phenotype.


## Step 1. Enrichment score

The enrichment scores are first computed for every single sample 
with the Bioconductor `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("GSVA")` 
package [@Hanzelmann2013]. Those scores represent the real score for each 
sample. Later steps treat this real score as the anchor point around which 
uncertainty gets modeled.

## Step 2. Permutation

Random subsets of samples, of fixed size, from the full dataset are 
repetitively drawn. For each of these resampled subsets, the enrichment score 
for the samples present are recomputed.

This step enables a per-sample uncertainty estimation (standard deviation).

## Step 3. Upscaling 

For each sample, a fixed number of simulated enrichment scores are drawn 
from a normal distribution centered on the real score, using the standard 
deviation estimated from permutations.

This step enables the upscaling of the total number of values that will 
be used in the next step. 

## Step 4. Mixture model

The synthetic values across all samples are pooled to fit two overlapping 
normal distributions to them. The two normal distributions are extracted using 
a mixture model approach implemented in the `r BiocStyle::CRANpkg("mixtools")`
package [@JSSv032i06]. The idea being that the whole cohort is actually a 
blend of two underlying populations (a "low enrichment" group and a 
"high enrichment" group). 
 

## Step 5. Classification

For each sample, a hypothesis testing whether its real score is consistent 
with belonging to the low-enrichment distribution.

For each sample, the pipeline runs a hypothesis test where the Null 
hypothesis (H₀) is that the sample actually belongs to the lower-enrichment 
distribution. The sample's real enrichment score (from Step 1) is checked 
against that null distribution. If the real score is implausible under the 
low-enrichment distribution (i.e., it falls somewhere that distribution 
would rarely produce), the null hypothesis is rejected. In that situation, the 
sample is classified as belonging to the higher-enrichment group which implies 
it is assigned to the tested signature. Otherwise, the sample is not 
classified. 

<br />


# Demonstration

For this demonstration, we are going to use the published RNA-seq dataset of 
pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) patients-derived organoids (PDOs) 
published in Tiriac et al. [@Tiriac2018]. The RNA-seq has been aligned with 
GENCODE v48 on GRCh38.p14 genome with STAR v2.7.9a [@Dobin2013]. Only one
PDO per patient was retained. The expected counts were processed with 
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("DESeq2")`  v1.50.2 [@Love2014] on genes expressed in at 
least 20% of the PDOs. The normalized expression is available in a 
_SummarizedExperiment_ object. 

In PDAC, the basal-like and classical subtypes, as defined in Moffitt et 
al [@Moffitt2015], are the two consistently employed molecular subtypes. The 
classical signature is associated to better prognosis and better response to 
standard chemotherapy while the basal-like subtype is associated 
with worse overall prognosis [@Moffitt2015, @OKane2020].

<br />

## Prepare the signatures

The basal-like and classical gene signatures are the one defined for 
PDOs in Tiriac et al. [@Tiriac2018]. 

```{r geneSignatures, echo=TRUE}

## Require package
library(splitTypeR)

## Prepare the PDOs basal-like and classical signatures
signaturesList <- list()
signaturesList[["Basal-like"]] <- 
        getGenesInSignature("2018_Tiriac_PDAC_PDO_basal-like_signature")
signaturesList[["Classical"]] <- 
        getGenesInSignature("2018_Tiriac_PDAC_PDO_classical_signature")

```

<br />

## Prepare the log2-transformed normalized expected counts

A matrix of normalized expected counts is required. The row are the genes while 
the patients (samples) are the columns.

The row annotation must correspond to the signature format. As an example, if 
the signatures are composed of gene names, the row annotation for the 
normalized expected counts must also be gene names.

For GSVA analysis, the normalized expected counts should be log-transformed to 
enable the use of the Gaussian distribution function. The current 
behavior of GSVA is to automatically choose one of the available distribution 
functions. 


```{r expCount, echo=TRUE}

## Required package
library(SummarizedExperiment)

## Load the SummarizedExperiment object
path <- system.file("extdata", "Tiriac_NormExpCounts.RDS", 
                        package="splitTypeR")
se <- readRDS(path)

## Extract the normalized counts and assign the gene names as row names
## The row names should correspond to the information present in the 
## gene signatures. In this case, the gene names are used. 
normCounts <- assays(se)[["normalizedCounts"]]
rownames(normCounts) <- rowRanges(se)$gene_name

## Log2-transform the data, adding a small pseudo-count to 
## prevent log2(0) errors 
log2normCounts <- log2(normCounts + 1)

```

<br />

## Run the subtyping method

The _runSubtypingBimodal_ function runs all the steps.

```{r subtyping, echo=TRUE}

## Fix seed for reproducible results
set.seed(81)

## Run the subtyping method using the log2-transformed data
result <- runSubtypingBimodal(geneLists=signaturesList, 
  expectedCountsMatrixLog=log2normCounts,
  permRatio=0.75,
  permNbr=20,
  upscaleNbr=12)

## Summary of the classification results
print(result)

```

<br />

The resulting object contains information from each step of the process. 
The information can be accessed using the appropriate getter function.

<br />

```{r signaturesGetter, echo=TRUE}
## Get the list of genes in each signature
signatures(result)
```

<br />

```{r gsvaResultsGetter, echo=TRUE}
## Get the GSVA scores for all samples in each signature
gsvaResults(result)
```

<br />

```{r permutationGetter, echo=TRUE}
## Get the GSVA scores for the first 5 samples in the first 8 permutations done 
## for the classical signature
permutations(result)[['Classical']][seq_len(5), seq_len(8)]
```

<br />

```{r standardDeviationGetter, echo=TRUE}
## Get the standard deviation for the GSVA scores for all samples in each 
## signature 
## The standard deviation is inferred from the permutation step
standardDeviation(result)
```

<br />

```{r upscalingGetter, echo=TRUE}
## Get the first 8 upscaling GSVA scores for the first 5 samples for the 
## classical signature 
upscaling(result)[['Classical']][seq_len(5), seq_len(8)]
```

<br />

```{r modelGetter, echo=TRUE}
## Get the mixture model for the classical signature
## This is a mixEM object
classicalModel <- model(result)[['Classical']]

## Get the two distribution means
classicalModel$mu
```

<br />

```{r classificatonGetter, echo=TRUE}
## Get the final classification of the samples for  the classical signature
classification(result)[['Classical']]
```


<br />

## Visual representation of the results at the permutation step

The _plotPermutationSamplesDistribution()_ function enables the visualization 
of the GSVA results obtained during the permutation step for a specific 
signature and specific samples. 

```{r graphPermutation, echo=TRUE}

## The GSVA results obtained for three samples during the permutation step 
## for the classical signature
## The seed is fixed to ensure reproducibility
plotPermutationSamplesDistribution(x=result, signature="Classical", 
    pointColor="darkorange", alpha=1, samples=c("hF23", "hT82", "hT89"), 
    seed=121)

```

<br />

## Visual representation of the results at the upscaling step

From the permutation step, the standard deviation is calculated for each 
samples. The upscaling is done with the real GSVA score as mean and the 
calculated standard deviation.

The _plotPermutationSamplesNormal()_ function shows the GSVA scores sampled 
during the upscaling step. The mean is shown as a vertical dotted line while 
the normal distribution is shown as a dashed line. The samples GSVA scores 
are shown as dots in this graph.

```{r graphUp, echo=TRUE}

## Fix seed for reproducibility
set.seed(121)

## The GSVA scores sampled for three samples during the upscaling step 
## for the classical signature
plotPermutationSamplesNormal(result, signature="Classical", 
    samples=c("hF23", "hT82", "hT89"), pointColor="darkviolet")
```

<br />

## Visual representation of the results at the mixture model step

The _plotDensityWithUpscalingSamplesBimodal()_ function enables the 
visualization of the two normal distributions obtained for a specific 
signature. In this graph, the GSVA values are the one obtained from the 
upscaling step.

```{r graphDensity, echo=TRUE}

plotDensityWithUpscalingSamplesBimodal(breaks = 26L,
    signature="Basal-like", result)

plotDensityWithUpscalingSamplesBimodal(breaks = 26L,
    signature="Classical", result)

```

<br />

## Classification of the samples

Let's compare the classification obtained here with the one from 
Tiriac et al. [@Tiriac2018].


```{r classifcationTiriac, echo=TRUE}

## Assignments from Tiriac et al
tiriacAssign <- read.table("Moffitt_Tiriac_Assignation.txt", sep="\t",
                                    header=TRUE)

## Assignments from the mixture model are extracted from the result
## By default, the samples are considered unclassified
## The samples are classified only if they are assign to one of the signatures
## When assigned to both signatures, the samples remain unclassified
assignation <- data.frame(
        Samples=rownames(classification(result)[['Classical']]), 
        newAssignation="unclassified")
assignation$Classical <- classification(result)[['Classical']]$classification
assignation$Basal <- classification(result)[['Basal-like']]$classification
assignation$newAssignation[which(assignation$Classical == "Classical" & 
                    assignation$Basal == "unclassified")] <- "Classical"
assignation$newAssignation[which(assignation$Basal == "Basal-like" & 
                    assignation$Classical == "unclassified")] <- "Basal-like"

## Merge the current assignments with the Tiriac et al. assignments into 
## one data frame
assignation <- merge(assignation[, c("Samples", "newAssignation")], 
                     tiriacAssign, by.x="Samples", 
                     by.y="Line", all.y=FALSE, all.x=FALSE)

table(assignation$newAssignation, assignation$Moffitt)
```

<br />

More than 85% of the samples (32 out of 37) are assigned the same subtype.

```{r compared, echo=TRUE}

gsva <- data.frame(Classical=classification(result)[['Classical']]$GSVA_score, 
                   Basal=classification(result)[['Basal-like']]$GSVA_score, 
                   row.names=rownames(classification(result)[['Basal-like']]))

retained <- assignation$Samples[which(assignation$newAssignation != 
                                            assignation$Moffitt)]

```
